domain: Political History / Institutional Change / Modernization Theory
topic_summary: Analysis of the Meiji government's 1872-1873 calendar reform (lunisolar to Gregorian) and 1870-1886 dress reform (traditional to Western), examining whether these constituted top-down exogenous imposition or endogenous displacement. The case tests whether commitment system vocabulary can capture forced institutional change where the prior system persists in practice despite legal abolition, creating stratified temporality rather than clean displacement.

key_entities: Meiji Government Oligarchy (Ōkubo Toshimichi, samurai-descended reformers)
Ministry of Finance (fiscal implementer; 13-month salary burden driver)
Kazoku/Former Samurai (resisted Western dress as status threat)
International System (Western powers; diplomatic/economic alignment pressure)
key_tensions: Official/Public vs Private/Rural Practice (nijuu seikatsu double life)
Fiscal Efficiency vs Cultural Continuity (13-month salary vs traditional festivals)
Geopolitical Positioning vs Endogenous Preference (datsu-A nyū-Ō vs actual demand)
Elite Status Markers vs Modernization Imperative (samurai dress resistance)
key_mechanisms: Imperial Edict Enforcement (1871-1886 dress codes; 1872 calendar decree)
Rhetorical Legitimation (Western dress framed as return to Emperor Jimmu era)
Fiscal Coercion (calendar switch eliminated intercalary month salary payment)
key_absences: No institutional mechanism for bottom-up input or consent in reform design
No category in standard modernization frameworks for enforced coexistence (stratified temporality where official system overlays but does not displace prior practice)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The legitimate basis for temporal coordination and social presentation — what grounds the authority to declare 'this is the correct calendar' or 'this is proper dress for public life'
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Meiji oligarchy claimed interpretive legitimacy through imperial symbolism (Emperor's personal adoption) and geopolitical necessity (alignment with Western powers for survival)
commitment_system_recognition.kernel_collapse_reason: Initial hypothesis: two readings (endogenous climb vs exogenous imposition) would emit different constraints. Actual finding: the Meiji case is NOT a contested kernel because there is no shared commitment being read differently. The prior system (lunisolar calendar, traditional dress) and the imposed system (Gregorian calendar, Western dress) are not two readings of one kernel — they are two separate kernels in forced coexistence. The 'contest' is not interpretive (how to read a shared commitment) but territorial (which kernel has authority in which domain). The oligarchy did not reinterpret the lunisolar calendar; it legally abolished it while lacking enforcement capacity to eliminate practice. This is institutional override, not kernel contestation. The structural phenomenon is stratified authority (official vs private domains operating under different kernels), not plural readings of one kernel.

omegas.description: Standard commitment system vocabulary lacks category for 'enforced coexistence' or 'stratified temporality' — where top-down imposition creates institutional bifurcation (official/public vs private/rural) rather than displacement. The Meiji case is not a contested kernel (no shared commitment being read differently) but rather two separate kernels in forced coexistence under asymmetric enforcement capacity. This suggests need for new category: 'territorial kernel contest' where authority domains rather than interpretive readings are contested.
omegas.source: §1.3-K kernel/reading decomposition; research context absence inventory

omegas.description: At what enforcement capacity does top-down imposition achieve displacement vs stratification? Meiji government could abolish legally but not eliminate practice. Is there a measurable threshold (state penetration ratio, rural/urban population distribution, communication infrastructure density) that predicts bifurcation vs displacement outcomes?
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) — no mechanism specified for enforcement capacity limits

omegas.description: How long does stratified coexistence persist? Research notes 'decades' of continued lunisolar observance but does not specify convergence timeline or conditions. Does stratification eventually collapse to displacement, or does it stabilize as permanent dual-system equilibrium?
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) — rural populations bear navigation costs indefinitely?

omegas.description: Standard modernization theory assumes either endogenous adoption (demonstration effects) or complete displacement. The Meiji case fits neither. Is this a general blind spot in modernization frameworks, or is Meiji an outlier case? Cross-domain comparison needed (e.g., Soviet calendar reform, French Revolutionary calendar, Turkish script reform).
omegas.source: F34 (Epistemic Trespass) — model's training on modernization theory may not cover coercion-driven institutional change adequately

fracture_scan.notes: F34 detected: Model's training on modernization theory and institutional change may not adequately cover coercion-driven top-down imposition cases. The research context provides strong empirical grounding, but the analytical framework (endogenous vs exogenous displacement) may be under-theorized in training data. Generated omega_modernization_framework_bias to bound this uncertainty. Additionally, the kernel/reading decomposition revealed that the initial 'contested kernel' hypothesis was incorrect — this is not interpretive contestation but territorial authority bifurcation, suggesting the kernel vocabulary itself has a gap (omega_kernel_vocabulary_gap).
